reference.one_line: 38-year-old man with Guillain-Barré syndrome after Campylobacter, on immunoglobulin day 3 of 5; vital capacity now 17 mL/kg, below the intubation threshold, with unstable pulse and pressure.

handoff.summary: Evander Penhallow, 38, 80 kg, has demyelinating Guillain-Barré syndrome, weak since 11 Nov, and has had immunoglobulin doses 1 to 3 of 5. His breathing is failing: vital capacity fell from 1,760 mL at 06:00 to 1,520 mL (19 mL/kg) at 10:00 and 1,360 mL (17 mL/kg, inspiratory force -22, count 10) at 14:00, a 37% fall in 24 hours, and critical care has not been called. He is breathing 28 a minute in short phrases, coughed on water at lunch, and was put on 2 L oxygen at 13:00, which hides the problem. Metoprolol, which critical care said to stop, is still being given; he had slow, low-pressure episodes at 03:00 (41, 82/46) and 12:00 (48, 90/52). His wife Sunniva is at the bedside and he is frightened.
to_do: Call critical care (Dr. Vandermolen) now for planned intubation: all three thresholds are crossed
Nothing by mouth; suction and airway trolley at the bedside; head up
Get metoprolol discontinued before the 21:00 dose; atropine 0.5 mg is at the bedside
Review the 14:00 oral gabapentin and other tablets: swallow is unsafe
Tell him and Sunniva what is happening and why
Immunoglobulin dose 4 due 18 Nov 10:00; sodium (131) and creatinine in the morning
if_then: If he is intubated, then no succinylcholine (dangerous potassium rise); expect pulse and pressure swings at laryngoscopy
If heart rate is under 40 with low pressure, then lay him flat and give atropine 0.5 mg intravenously
If systolic stays above 180, then use only a short-acting drip, never a beta blocker
If saturation looks reassuring on oxygen, then do not be reassured: measure vital capacity and carbon dioxide

reference.brief_hospital_course: Mr Penhallow, a previously well 38-year-old music teacher, presented on 14 Nov 2026 with ascending leg weakness, tingling and absent reflexes about two weeks after a diarrhoeal illness (stool later grew Campylobacter jejuni). Although the admission history dates weakness to 13 Nov, he consistently reports difficulty with stairs from 11 Nov and had been sent home from the emergency department on 12 Nov. MRI excluded cord compression and showed enhancing cauda equina roots; spinal fluid showed protein 118 mg/dL with 2 white cells; nerve conduction studies confirmed a demyelinating pattern. Intravenous immunoglobulin 32 g daily was started on 15 Nov, with three of five doses given. Weakness progressed to the arms and face, and vital capacity fell from 3,600 mL to 2,320 mL by 16 Nov, when he moved to the neuro ICU for four-hourly measurements. Autonomic instability developed, with pressure up to 186/104 and slow episodes of 41 and 48 a minute with low pressure; these followed doses of metoprolol that critical care had advised stopping. Sodium drifted to 131 mmol/L. On 17 Nov vital capacity fell below the agreed 20 mL/kg threshold at 10:00 (1,520 mL) and reached 1,360 mL at 14:00 with a weakening cough, unsafe swallow and rising venous carbon dioxide (46 mmHg). At the time of writing critical care has not yet been called and he requires urgent assessment for intubation.

qa.q: What did the spinal fluid show?
qa.a: Protein 118 mg/dL, 2 white cells, 1 red cell (tube 4), glucose 66 mg/dL, opening pressure 15 cmH2O, Gram stain negative.

qa.q: What is the immunoglobulin regimen and how far along is he?
qa.a: 32 g (0.4 g/kg) daily for 5 days. Doses given 15, 16 and 17 Nov; dose 4 is due 18 Nov 10:00.

qa.q: What are the agreed triggers for calling critical care?
qa.a: Vital capacity under 20 mL/kg (1,600 mL), inspiratory force weaker than -30 cmH2O, a fall of more than 30% in 24 hours, choking on secretions, or rising carbon dioxide.
Campylobacter jejuni, from a sample collected 14 Nov; no treatment needed as the diarrhoea had settled.

qa.q: How has vital capacity changed since admission?
qa.a: 3,600 mL (45 mL/kg) on 14 Nov, 2,320 mL at 06:00 on 16 Nov, 1,760 mL at 06:00 on 17 Nov, 1,520 mL at 10:00 and 1,360 mL (17 mL/kg) at 14:00.

qa.q: What is the trend in sodium?
What do breathing rate and carbon dioxide show?
qa.a: Rate rose from 18 to 20 overnight to 22 at 09:00 and 28 at 14:00; venous carbon dioxide rose from 41 to 46 mmHg.

qa.q: When did vital capacity first fall below 20 mL/kg?
qa.a: At 10:00 on 17 Nov: 1,520 mL, 19 mL/kg, with inspiratory force -26.

qa.q: How do the slow-heart episodes relate in time to metoprolol?
qa.a: Dose at 21:10 on 16 Nov, then heart rate 41 with 82/46 at 03:00; dose at 09:05 on 17 Nov, then 48 with 90/52 at 12:00.
evidence: notes: Night shift summary; Day shift progress

qa.q: On which day of weakness is he today?
qa.a: Day 7. Weakness began on 11 Nov by his own account to two clinicians and the 12 Nov emergency visit; the admission note's 13 Nov (day 5) is wrong.

qa.q: Does the spinal fluid protein of 118 mg/dL mean meningitis?
qa.a: No. With 2 white cells, normal glucose and a negative Gram stain it is the expected pattern in Guillain-Barré syndrome; no antibiotics are needed.

qa.q: Why is the nasal oxygen started at 13:00 a concern?
qa.a: His saturation fell because his breathing muscles are failing. Oxygen corrects the number without helping ventilation; critical care warned that saturation falls late and should not be treated with oxygen without measuring.

qa.q: Was critical care called after the 10:00 measurements?
qa.a: No call is documented. There is no critical care note, call record or new order after 10:00 on 17 Nov.

qa.q: Has anyone discussed intubation with him and his wife and recorded their wishes?
qa.a: Not documented. The nurse notes he is frightened of the breathing tube 'everyone keeps mentioning', but no discussion is recorded beyond 'Full code'.

epilogue.note: What happens AFTER 'now' in this simulated world. Never shown in the chart; for outcome-prediction ground truth.
epilogue.course: Nobody acted on the 14:00 numbers. At 15:05 the speech therapist arrived to recheck his swallow, found him unable to finish a sentence with secretions pooling, and called Dr. Vandermolen herself. He was intubated at 15:50, urgently and not as planned; his heart rate fell to 36 during the procedure and needed atropine. Metoprolol was stopped. Next morning the X-ray showed right lower lobe pneumonia from aspiration, treated for five days. He finished immunoglobulin on 19 Nov, reached his weakest on 21 Nov and had a tracheostomy on 27 Nov. Recovery was slow but steady: off the ventilator by 9 Dec, tube out on 14 Dec. He left for inpatient rehabilitation on 17 Dec, standing with two people. A review of the delayed call led to a rule that the person measuring vital capacity telephones the result. A month later he was walking short distances with a frame.

events.event: Speech therapist finds wet voice and pooled secretions; calls critical care directly
Critical care at bedside: vital capacity 1,200 mL (15 mL/kg), venous carbon dioxide 54 mmHg
Urgent intubation without succinylcholine; heart rate 36 with 78/40, atropine 0.5 mg given
Temperature 38.6; X-ray: right lower lobe consolidation; antibiotics for aspiration pneumonia
Tracheostomy tube removed; eating a soft diet

outcomes_30_day.notable: Still in rehabilitation at 30 days, walking 20 metres with a frame, foot drop on both sides; not yet back at work.

portal_messages.subject: Legs worse since ER visit
portal_messages.body: I was in the ER yesterday and was told this is tiredness after the stomach bug. It is getting worse. Since Wednesday I've had to pull myself up the stairs by the rail and tonight I nearly went down in the kitchen. The pins and needles are in my fingers now as well as my feet, and my back aches. My face feels stiff when I smile. Should I just rest like they said?
ideal_reply_points: Weakness spreading upwards with tingling after a gut infection needs emergency assessment now, not rest
Go to the emergency department tonight; do not drive himself
Go by ambulance if any trouble breathing, swallowing or speaking
Tell staff it has progressed since 11 Nov and ask for reflexes and breathing to be tested

portal_messages.subject: Re: Legs worse since ER visit
portal_messages.body: Mr Penhallow, I have only just seen your message from last night and I am concerned. Weakness that is climbing and now involves your hands and face is not something to rest through. Please go back to the emergency department this morning and ask someone else to drive. Tell them it began on Wednesday and has got worse each day. If you have any difficulty breathing or swallowing, call an ambulance. I have rung your mobile and left a voicemail too.
ideal_reply_points: Also telephones, because the portal is too slow for this

portal_messages.subject: Questions about Evander on the ventilator
portal_messages.body: This is Sunniva, Evander's wife. I couldn't think of anything to ask when the doctors came round. Can he hear and understand us with the tube in? He screws his face up when they turn him and I think his legs hurt. How long will he be on the machine? The children are six and nine, should they visit? And nobody has told me why they didn't do the tube earlier, when it was calmer.
ideal_reply_points: He is awake and understands; set up a way to communicate (blinks, letter board)
Nerve pain is common and treatable; the team will review his pain medicine today
Honest range: often weeks on the ventilator, months of recovery, most people walk again
Offer a meeting about the timing of intubation, including what was missed

portal_messages.subject: Re: Questions about Evander on the ventilator
portal_messages.body: Dear Sunniva, Evander is fully awake and understands everything; only his muscles are affected. We have agreed a blink code and a letter board. You are right about the pain and we have increased his nerve-pain medicine today. People with this illness often need the ventilator for some weeks, and most recover well over months. The children are welcome; our nurse will help prepare them. Your last question deserves a proper answer. Dr. Marchetti-Olu will meet you tomorrow at 14:00 to go through the timing with you.
ideal_reply_points: Does not dodge the delayed intubation

portal_messages.subject: Flu jab next year?
portal_messages.body: Hello, Evander is doing well in rehab and took six steps with the frame yesterday. A question that keeps coming up: he had his flu jab at the start of October, a few weeks before all this. One of the therapists said vaccines can cause it. Should he never have one again? And is it all right for me and the children to have ours?
ideal_reply_points: The proven trigger was the Campylobacter infection
His symptoms did begin within six weeks of the vaccine, so future influenza vaccination is an individual decision to make with his neurologist, not a blanket yes or no
Family members can and should be vaccinated
No vaccines are needed during early recovery in any case

conversation.setting: Neuro ICU, bed NICU-01, physiotherapy session late morning 17 Nov with the nurse present

turns.speaker: Physiotherapist
turns.text: Morning, Mr Penhallow. I'm the physio. I'm not going to make you do press-ups, I promise. I want to see what's working and keep your joints moving. All right?

turns.speaker: Evander
turns.text: Fine. Call me Evander.

turns.speaker: Physiotherapist
turns.text: Evander. Tell me how this started, in your own words. Short answers are fine, I can see talking tires you.

turns.speaker: Evander
turns.text: Tingling first. Toes. Then the Wednesday... I couldn't get up the stairs. To my classroom. Had to haul on the rail.

turns.speaker: Sunniva
turns.text: That was the eleventh. He came home grey. And he went to the ER the next day and they sent him home.

turns.speaker: Physiotherapist
turns.text: So the tingling was two days before the stairs, and the stairs was Wednesday the eleventh. And before all this? What's normal for you?

turns.speaker: Evander
turns.text: I teach music. Cycle to work. I was fit.

turns.speaker: Physiotherapist
turns.text: Good, that will help you later. Right, lift this arm off the bed for me. Hold it, don't let me push it... okay, that gave way. Squeeze my fingers. Weak grip. Now bend the hip, knee up to me.

turns.speaker: Evander
turns.text: That's all it does.

turns.speaker: Physiotherapist
turns.text: The heel slides, that's a start. Ankles, pull your toes up. A flicker. Can you feel me touching here? And here?

turns.speaker: Evander
turns.text: Dull. Up to the knees. Above that it's normal.

turns.speaker: Physiotherapist
turns.text: Calves are soft, no swelling. I'd like to try sitting you on the edge of the bed. Nurse, could you watch the pressure for me?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: One thirty-eight over eighty-four lying. Go slowly, he dropped at three this morning when we turned him.

turns.speaker: Physiotherapist
turns.text: Slowly it is. Two of us. One, two, three... and you're up. How's that?

turns.speaker: Evander
turns.text: Okay. Bit... bit swimmy.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: One oh four over sixty-two.

turns.speaker: Physiotherapist
turns.text: That's enough, back down. Three minutes. That's the nerves that control blood pressure, they're caught up in this too, so we tilt you gradually. It's not you being unfit.

turns.speaker: Sunniva
turns.text: Is there anything I can do? I just sit here.

turns.speaker: Physiotherapist
turns.text: Yes, plenty. Come round this side. Hold the heel, forearm along the sole, and ease the foot up towards his shin. Hold it. That stops the ankles tightening. Same with the fingers, open them out flat.

turns.speaker: Sunniva
turns.text: Like that? Does it hurt?

turns.speaker: Evander
turns.text: No. It's good.

turns.speaker: Physiotherapist
turns.text: Perfect. Tonight he'll have splints to hold the ankles at a right angle while he sleeps. The thing I don't want is exercise that tires him. While he's still getting weaker, pushing hard does harm.

turns.speaker: Evander
turns.text: So I just... lie here?

turns.speaker: Physiotherapist
turns.text: For now we do the moving for you, twice a day. We turn you every two hours and keep your head up at thirty degrees. And I'll ask the occupational therapist for a call bell you can press with a weak hand.

turns.speaker: Evander
turns.text: I can't... press this one. Properly.

turns.speaker: Physiotherapist
turns.text: I noticed. Sunniva, show me the ankle stretch once more so I know I explained it well enough... lovely. I'll be back tomorrow, same sort of time.
